title: Foundation Models Enabling Multi-Scale Battery Materials Discovery: From Molecules To Devices
experiments_summary: The study evaluated multiple foundation models (FMs) and Morgan Fingerprints (MF) across ten battery-related datasets spanning molecular, formulation, and device scales. The FMs assessed included SMI-TED (pre-trained on 91 million SMILES), MolT5 (pre-trained on 100 million SMILES with natural language descriptions), Galactica (pre-trained on broad scientific literature including SMILES), and GraphMVP (graph-based model using 2D and 3D molecular representations), with MF serving as the benchmark. A transfer learning approach was used: pre-trained FM embeddings were extracted for individual molecules, then scaled by molar composition and aggregated (via scaled addition) to form formulation or device-level descriptors. Additional extrinsic variables (temperature, separator label, cathode loading) were concatenated to these descriptors as appropriate. Feed-forward neural networks were individually optimized per dataset and trained on these aggregated features. Training and evaluation used five independent 80%-20% train-test splits, with mean absolute error (MAE) as the primary metric. Datasets included: molecular properties from D3TaLES (40,000 DFT-computed values), electrolyte solubility (3,300 data points from laboratory experiments combining single-salt/single-solvent, single-salt/multi-solvent, and multi-salt/multi-solvent systems), ionic conductivity (18,000 empirical values at varying temperatures), contact angle on four Celgard separators (119 in-house measurements using sessile drop technique), Coulombic Efficiency (150 data points), LiI battery specific capacity (125 data points), and Li-ICl battery capacity (91 data points with cathode loading and separator variations). Out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization was assessed by analyzing prediction error as a function of chemical similarity between train and test sets. Interpretability was investigated by defining over 550 chemical substructures via SMARTS strings, encoding their presence in formulations as composition-scaled fingerprint vectors, and computing Spearman correlation coefficients between these chemical moieties and both actual and FM-predicted outcomes across CE, LiI capacity, and ionic conductivity datasets. Fine-tuning versus transfer learning was also compared on the ionic conductivity dataset using mean squared error.
